description: We are Lyra, a team of four Software Engineering students tackling the Space Mission Design Game challenge. Named after the compact northern constellation anchored by Vega (one of the brightest stars in the sky and a foundational reference point in astronomy) our goal is to build an interactive simulation where players manage real spaceflight engineering trade-offs, from mass and power budgets to orbital mechanics and mission design.
summary: Mission Stella is a 2D educational space game for children aged 8 to 15, set in the Taquari Valley, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil. Players lead a young space agency and use satellite technology to solve four real problems of local communities: crop pests, landslide risk, lack of rural internet, and fires/deforestation. In each mission the player talks to a resident, builds a satellite (battery, computer, communication, sensor) under a budget, passes a mini-game inspired by a real NASA instrument (Landsat, NISAR, SCaN/TDRS, FIRMS), launches it and sees the impact on the region. The game shows that space data is not only for looking at stars: it affects food, safety, communication and the environment in everyday life. It also displays real-time weather for the player's city through APIs, teaching how data-driven decisions work. Available in English and Portuguese, free, with no ads or chat, and ready for classroom use.
details:
WHAT IT IS

Mission Stella (internal name: Missão Taquari) is a browser-based 2D educational exploration and simulation game created by Team Lyra for children and teenagers aged 8 to 15. It is set in the Taquari Valley, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, and shows how satellite data from space agencies like NASA helps ordinary people in everyday life: the food we eat, the safety of our homes, rural internet access and the protection of the environment.

HOW IT WORKS

The player is a young leader of a space agency and completes four community missions:

1. Operation Fertile Soil: a pest attacks corn and soybean crops. Ideal sensor: multispectral camera. Mini-game inspired by Landsat NDVI.

2. Operation Hillside Sentinel: heavy rain threatens landslides. Ideal sensor: SAR radar. Mini-game inspired by NISAR.

3. Operation Taquari Connection: rural schools and farms have no internet. Ideal sensor: Ku-band transponder. Mini-game inspired by NASA SCaN/TDRS telemetry.

4. Operation Guardian of Waters and Forests: fires and deforestation threaten the riparian forests. Ideal sensor: thermal infrared. Mini-game inspired by NASA FIRMS (MODIS/VIIRS).

Each mission follows a three-stage loop: Plan on Earth (talk to a resident and understand the problem), Accomplish in space (build a satellite with a 1,000-credit budget, pass the scientific challenge and launch), and Impact (see how the solution helps the region and learn the science behind it). Engineering trade-offs such as energy, reliability, mass and cost determine the mission success chance, and failed missions can be retried, teaching that engineers learn from failure.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Players learn what remote sensing is, why different sensors solve different problems, the basic parts of a satellite (power, computer, communication, sensor), and how real weather data reaches us through APIs. The game connects NASA science to the player's own region and makes space feel useful and close to home. It is free, has no ads and no chat, collects only a nickname and a city, works in English and Portuguese, and is designed for classroom use.

REAL DATA

The top bar shows real-time weather for the player's city (temperature, rain, humidity, wind, gusts, wind direction and pressure) from the Meteomatics Weather API. City search uses the Open-Meteo Geocoding API and place names come from the BigDataCloud Reverse Geocoding API. If credentials are unavailable, the game falls back to clearly marked simulated values so it never breaks.

NASA RESOURCES

NASA missions and instruments (Landsat, NISAR, SCaN/TDRS, Deep Space Network, GPM, FIRMS with MODIS/VIIRS) and NASA Worldview inspired the mission narratives, mini-games and the "Curiosities" section. The game does not download live NASA data. The mini-games are simplified educational simulations, and the community results shown after each mission are fictional and illustrative.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

HTML5 Canvas and plain JavaScript (front end), Node.js and Express (back end), Web Audio API (synthesized sounds), browser localStorage and a JSON file for saving progress, hosted on Vercel, with source code on GitHub.

CREATIVE ASPECTS

A local, culturally grounded setting with real cities of the Taquari Valley, a friendly star guide named Lyra, a drag-and-drop satellite workbench, four different mini-games, a shop and leaderboard, and a bilingual interface.

USE OF AI

Generative AI tools were used as a support tool during development (code assistance) and in writing documentation. All AI-assisted code and text was reviewed, adapted and approved by the team. The game does not call any AI service while running, and no NASA logos or branding were generated or modified. NASA names are used for educational purposes only; the project is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.
